description: Sentence Connectors are words or phrases that establish a logical relationship between two or more sentences or clauses. A strong grasp of connectors is essential in Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension to understand the author's flow of ideas and tone.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.description: Fundamental principles of sentence connectors and their significance in comprehension.

key_concepts.explanation: Connectors clarify the direction in which the author's thought process is moving. They provide a smooth transition from one idea to the next, indicating continuation, contrast, or conclusion.

When combining sentences, the original meaning and tone of the individual statements must remain completely unchanged. The choice of connector depends entirely on the underlying relationship between the sentences.

sections.title: Types of Connectors and Indicators
sections.description: Important connectors that represent different types of relationships and serve as critical clues in exams.

key_indicators.usage_hint: Used when two sentences present opposing or contradictory ideas. In RC, these indicate a shift in the author's perspective or tone.
Used when one sentence describes an action or event and the other describes its result or reason. Helpful in finding concluding sentences in Para Jumbles.
Used when the second sentence supports the idea of the first sentence or provides extra, parallel information in the same direction.
Used when the occurrence of one event is strictly dependent on the occurrence of another.

sections.title: Question Types
sections.description: The main formats of questions asked in competitive exams regarding connectors.

question_types.explanation: Two separate sentences are provided, and you must select the correct connector from the options to combine them into a single grammatically correct sentence.
question_types.approach: Identify the relationship between the two statements (e.g., cause, contrast, or addition) and select the connector that logically fits this relationship.

question_types.explanation: Options provide starter phrases or connectors. You must choose the starter that can combine the given sentences by placing the connector at the very beginning of the new sentence.
question_types.approach: Check which starter can weave both sentences together meaningfully without altering the original context or violating grammar rules.

question_types.explanation: Connectors act as direct transition clues to find the correct sequence or fill the correct blank.
question_types.approach: If a sentence begins with 'However' or 'Therefore', it cannot be the opening sentence. Look for the preceding idea that it contradicts or concludes.

sections.title: Grammar Rules and Usage
sections.description: Rules to avoid common grammatical errors when utilizing sentence connectors.

grammar_rules.explanation: The conjunction 'but' is never used with 'Although' or 'Though'. Instead, the clauses should be separated by a comma or the word 'yet'.

grammar_rules.structure: Despite + Noun / Gerund (without 'of') OR In spite of + Noun / Gerund
grammar_rules.explanation: The preposition 'of' is never used with 'Despite', whereas it is mandatory to use 'of' with 'In spite'. Both phrases mean exactly the same thing.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Although he was ill, but he attended the meeting.
examples.correct_or_usage: Although he was ill, he attended the meeting. (OR: Although he was ill, yet he attended the meeting.)
examples.explanation: According to grammar rules, using 'but' with 'Although' is incorrect.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Despite of working hard, she failed the exam.
examples.correct_or_usage: Despite working hard, she failed the exam. (OR: In spite of working hard, she failed the exam.)
examples.explanation: Using 'of' directly after 'Despite' is a common grammatical error.

sections.title: Solving Strategies
sections.description: Step-by-step strategies to improve accuracy and speed while solving connector questions.

strategies.title: Identify the Logical Relationship
strategies.detail: Read both sentences and determine if they are moving in the same direction (Positive-Positive / Negative-Negative) or opposing directions (Positive-Negative). For instance, if one sentence states a problem and the other offers a solution, you need a connector of contrast.

strategies.title: Process of Elimination
strategies.detail: Immediately eliminate connectors that imply the wrong relationship. If the relationship between the sentences is cause-and-effect, boldly cross out options containing 'However' or 'Moreover'.

strategies.title: Check Grammatical Structure
strategies.detail: After selecting a potential connector, read the combined sentence in your mind. Ensure that the new sentence is structurally sound, grammatically correct, and keeps the original meaning fully intact.
